entities.summary:
Petter Sørlle (1884–1933) was a pioneering Norwegian whaling captain and inventor whose innovative "slipway" technology fundamentally transformed pelagic whaling in the early 20th century. Born in Tønsberg, Norway, a hub of maritime enterprise, Sørlle's career coincided with the zenith of the industrial whaling era, where escalating demand for whale oil drove intense technological competition. His invention revolutionized the processing of whale carcasses at sea, moving it from dangerous, weather-dependent alongside operations to safer, more efficient onboard factory ship operations, thereby significantly increasing the scale and efficacy of the industry across the Southern Ocean.

Sørlle’s most significant contribution, the stern slipway, was first patented in 1922 and implemented aboard the factory ship *Lancing* in the 1925–26 Antarctic whaling season. This ingenious design allowed entire whale carcasses, often weighing hundreds of tons, to be hauled directly onto the deck of a factory ship through an opening in the stern. Previously, whales had to be flensed (skinned and butchered) while floating alongside the ship, a hazardous and time-consuming process heavily impacted by rough seas. The slipway enabled continuous processing regardless of weather conditions, drastically improving operational efficiency and safety for the crews. This innovation quickly became standard across the global whaling fleet, notably adopted by major Norwegian and British whaling companies operating in the Antarctic.
